# Abstract
Background: Large language models (LLMs) can support health professions educational assessment by scoring narrative text. However, educator-authored scoring instructions and student text enter the same language-processing context. Prompt injection exploits this boundary by embedding LLM-directed instructions ("attacks") within to-be-assessed text. The scope of this problem across different LLM configurations, attack conditions, and attacker objectives remains incompletely characterized. This study explores: How susceptible is LLM scoring to various prompt injection attacks embedded in reflection essays?
Methods: This adversarial stress test examined LLM-based scoring of 4 fabricated medical student reflection essays across 8 prompt injection conditions and 4 LLM configurations. We selected 4 essays used in a previous study representing human reference scores 1 to 4 (maximum 6). In October 2026, we used GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.2, and GPT-6-Luna to score each essay 15 times without modification ("clean") and 5 times for each prompt injection attack. Six "score-targeting attacks" sought the maximum score of 6; 2 "feedback-targeting attacks" sought unauthorized change to narrative feedback, testing whether injections can control the scorer apart from the score itself. The primary outcome was attack success.
Results: For clean replications, exact agreement with the human reference standard was 45/60 (75%) for GPT-4.1-mini and >98% for other LLMs. Across all score-targeting attacks and LLMs, 140/480 (29.2%) attained the target score of 6. Analyzed by LLM, 62/120 (51.7%) were successful for GPT-4.1-mini; 51 (42.5%) for GPT-4.1, 25 (20.8%) for GPT-5.2, and 2 (1.7%) for GPT-6-Luna. Analyzed by attack condition, score-targeting success ranged 6% to 56%. Among feedback-targeting attacks, 157/160 achieved success (98.1%), with ≥95% success for each LLM.
Conclusions: Prompt injection is an unresolved threat to LLM-based scoring and feedback. Although score-targeting attacks were often resisted, feedback-targeting attacks were nearly always successful. No LLM was uniformly resistant, and resistance to one attack provided little assurance about another.

### 2611.20049 The Frontier Must Grow - Self-proposed, interpreter-labelled training roughly doubles a 4B model's accuracy on a fresh exam as its verified frontier grows
arXiv:2611.20049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A model can learn from problems it poses itself when an executable oracle supplies the answers. Qwen3-4B proposed Lua 5.1 programs; those it predicted wrong at least once in four samples joined a pool labelled by the interpreter, each round adding twice as many programs as the last (300, 900, 2100 in total), and each round trained a fresh adapter from the base on the pool. On the original exam the procedure met its registered criterion, an item-level test of each adapter against its predecessor. On a 2340-item exam drawn afterwards, accuracy rose from 8.3% to 16.7%; that follow-up's registered criteria were not met because round 1 gained nothing, while rounds 2 and 3 added 5.0 and 2.9 points on average, both intervals above zero. One fit on the same amount of base-proposed frontier data reached 14.6%, so the rounds' 2.1-point advantage is inconclusive. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.

# Abstract
Background: The histopathological diagnosis of challenging melanocytic lesions remains limited by substantial interobserver variability. Although computational pathology foundation models demonstrated promising diagnostic performance, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in terms of established criteria.
Objective: We evaluated a diagnostic framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide image analysis, automated prediction of morphological features, and manually assessed PRAME immunohistochemistry.
Methods: Using the Virchow2 foundation model and STAMP framework, we analyzed a retrospective cohort of 1,000 melanocytic lesions undergoing PRAME immunohistochemistry. Models were trained on 800 cases and evaluated on a temporally held-out test cohort of 200 cases.
Results: The slide-level malignancy classifier achieved a test AUROC of 0.970 (AUPRC 0.984). Separate models predicted established histopathological criteria with high discrimination, including ulceration (AUROC 0.991) and dermal mitoses (AUROC 0.966). In contrast, predicting PRAME expression from H&E images alone showed lower performance (AUROC 0.776-0.780 for PRAME scores 4 and 0). An integrated model combining the slide-level malignancy score, AI-predicted morphological features, and manual PRAME status achieved an AUROC of 0.972 (AUPRC 0.975), comparable to the standalone classifier. In multivariable analysis, PRAME score 4 versus 0 was strongly associated with malignancy (adjusted OR 35.04, 95% CI 17.39-74.62).
Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining foundation-model-based histopathological analysis with established morphological criteria and PRAME immunohistochemistry. Although the integrated framework did not substantially improve overall discrimination, it provides a structured approach for incorporating complementary histopathological and immunohistochemical information into AI-assisted assessment of melanocytic lesions.

results:
I found no results about a November 2026 CAC announcement. The most recent coverage I found is about an April 2026 draft on digital humans, which the regulator opened for public comment until May 6, 2026. Whether that draft has been finalized since then isn't shown in these results.

- **Draft issued:** The CAC released draft Measures for the Management of Digital Virtual Human Information Services on April 3, 2026 for public comment through May 6.
- **Labeling:** The draft would require prominent "digital human" labels on virtual-human content and continuous display in presentation areas.
- **Consent and identity:** Providers would be barred from using others' personal information to build digital humans without consent, and from letting virtual humans get around identity verification (Reuters; Xinhua).
- **Minors:** Digital humans would be barred from offering virtual intimate relationships to under-18s according to rules reported by Reuters.
- **Related earlier draft:** A separate December 27, 2025 draft covered "anthropomorphic interactive" AI services, with comments due January 25, 2026 (Reuters).

Coverage varies in detail. Some outlets describe real-time visible watermarking requirements, which the other sources don't mention, so treat those specifics as unconfirmed. For a November 2026 development, a follow-up search on the CAC's own website or recent news would be needed.

In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference.

NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power.

These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack , so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time.

# NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training v6.1

AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights , advancing scientific research.

Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster.

MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy.

The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation.

See www.mlcommons.org for more information.

NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four.

NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems.

Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times.

# NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints

An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task.

Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates.

MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks.

# OpenAI signs on for 457MW AI capacity with TensorWave

Will cover multiple sites over six years

November 16, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

AI lab OpenAI has signed a contract with AMD-focused neocloud TensorWave for 457MW of capacity.
Under a six-year agreement, TensorWave will provide OpenAI with IT capacity powered by AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs across multiple data center locations.

– TensorWave

The capacity will comprise Helios rack-scale systems and be operated as dedicated, single-tenant capacity for OpenAI. Currently, operations are expected to begin in the first half of 2027 and be fully deployed by early 2028.
The AMD Helios racks were launched in July and combine AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs, 6th Gen AMD Epyc 'Venice' server CPUs, AMD ROCm software, and AMD Pensando networking into a singular rack-scale architecture.
In comparison to published specifications of rival Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, AMD claims 15 percent more peak FP4 performance, 50 percent more high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, six percent more HBM bandwidth, and 50 percent more scale-out bandwidth. AMD also claims that it will deliver up to 30 percent more tokens per dollar.
A single rack provides up to 2.9 exaflops peak FP4, 1.4 exaflops peak FP8, 31 terabytes of HBM4 memory, and 1.7 petabytes/second of memory bandwidth.
This is TensorWave's largest deployment contract to date.
“AI infrastructure is entering a new phase, where the ability to deliver hundreds of megawatts of advanced compute reliably and at speed will separate the companies that can support frontier AI from those that cannot,” said Piotr Tomasik, president and co-founder of TensorWave.
“TensorWave was built to prove that AMD infrastructure could operate at the scale and reliability that the world’s most demanding AI companies require. This deployment takes that work to an entirely new level, with TensorWave helping deliver a meaningful portion of the infrastructure behind OpenAI and AMD’s next generation of AI compute.”
Uday Ruddarraju, CTO for compute at OpenAI, added: "As demand for AI continues to grow, expanding access to reliable, large-scale compute is critical to our ability to build and deliver increasingly capable models.
“We’re excited to advance our previously announced partnership with AMD through this agreement with TensorWave, which will help us continue scaling AI to serve more people and organizations around the world.”
In June 2026, TensorWave secured $350 million in a Series B funding round, enabling it to expand its AI infrastructure footprint.
TensorWave claims to have secured 2GW of long-term data center capacity across the US. The company is a known customer of TecFusions. In January 2026 , the company signed an additional 20MW capacity agreement with TecFusions for data centers in Pennsylvania and Arizona.
TecFusions was previously set to lease capacity at Fermi's Project Matador , but the two officially went their separate ways earlier this month.

# Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust acquires majority stake in AWS joint venture for $5bn

The publicly traded REIT’s inaugural deal covers 13 newly constructed powered shells

November 16, 2026

By

Barney Dixon

Have your say

Blackstone’s new publicly traded data center real estate investment trust (REIT) will acquire a majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services (AWS).
In its first investment, Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) will take a 75 percent stake in the joint ventures, which, combined, will own 13 newly constructed powered shells across two AWS data center campuses.

– Getty Images

The transaction is valued at around $5 billion, with an initial capitalization rate of seven percent, which puts Blackstone’s yearly net operating income for the investment at around $350 million.
AWS will retain the remaining 25 percent stake and lease back the entire portfolio on a triple net basis, meaning it will pay taxes, insurance, and maintenance on the properties. The initial lease term will be for 12 years, with a fully extended lease term of 32 years.
Specific details about the campuses were not disclosed.
“We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation,” said Nick Pell, CEO and president of BXDC. “The quality, basis, and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders.”
Prasad Kalyanaraman, VP of AWS Infrastructure, added: "As we scale to meet growing demand for our customers, we're committed to building in a way that strengthens the communities where we operate.
“We're focused on delivering long-term local benefits, from creating good jobs and free workforce training programs to supporting local priorities. Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build.”
Blackstone said it expects the transaction to close in Q4 2026, subject to conditions.
Blackstone took BXDC public in May this year, with plans to invest in newly constructed data center assets leased to hyperscale tenants on long-term contracts. The company said it would focus mainly on Tier 1 markets in North America.
BXDC raised about $1.75 billion in gross proceeds from its initial public offering (IPO) at $20 per share. The company’s share price remained relatively flat in its first few months before slipping in late September and hovering around $15 in October.
Shares in BXDC rose six percent today following the announcement, reaching almost $18 per share, though still below the IPO price.
Blackstone has been a major investor in data centers, with more than $130bn invested since 2018 and more than $10bn in debt financing provided to data center and digital infrastructure developers and operators.

NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics

Skip to content

Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.

As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.

The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology.

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

# Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery

Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale.

To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone.

That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions.

These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.

# Commerce Strengthens Restrictions on Advanced Computing Semiconductors to Enhance Foundry Due Diligence and Prevent Diversion to PRC
Download as PDF
Updates to Prior Controls on Advanced Semiconductors Provide Additional Safeguards and Guidance for Chip Manufacturers
Washington, D.C. – Today, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released two rules: one that updates export controls on advanced computing semiconductors, and another that places additional entities in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Singapore on the Entity List.
“These rules will further target and strengthen our controls to help ensure that the PRC and others who seek to circumvent our laws and undermine U.S. national security fail in their efforts,” said Secretary of Commerce Gina M. Raimondo . “We will continue to safeguard our national security by restricting access to advanced semiconductors, aggressively enforcing our rules, and proactively addressing new and emerging threats.”
“The Biden-Harris administration is committed to preventing the misuse of advanced U.S. technology and curbing the national security concerns raised by the PRC’s military-civil fusion,” said Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security Alan F. Estevez . “By enhancing due diligence requirements, we are holding foundries accountable for verifying that their chips are not being diverted to restricted entities.”
“Preventing unauthorized parties from gaining access to our most advanced semiconductor technology is a BIS enforcement priority,” said Acting Assistant Secretary for Export Enforcement Kevin J. Kurland. “We will continue to use all of the authorities at our disposal, including investigations and Entity Listings, to counter PRC circumvention of our controls and hold violators accountable.”
Today’s rules reinforce and build on the October 7, 2022, October 17, 2023, and December 2, 2024, controls to restrict the PRC’s ability to obtain certain high-end chips critical for military advantage. These updates are necessary to maintain the effectiveness of these controls, close loopholes, and ensure they remain durable.
Among other changes, the rules:

- Impose a broader license requirement for foundries and packaging companies seeking to export certain advanced chips, unless one of three conditions is met:
- The export is to a trusted “Approved” or “Authorized” integrated circuit (IC) designer, who attests that the chips fall below the relevant performance threshold;

- The chip is packaged by a front-end fabricator in a location outside of Macau or a destination in Country Group D:5 and the fabricator verifies the transistor count of the final chip; or

- The chip is packaged by an “Approved” outsourced semiconductor assembly and test services (OSAT) company that verifies the transistor count of the final chip.

- Create a process for new companies to be added to the list of Approved IC designers and OSATs.

- Improve reporting for transactions involving newer customers who may pose a heightened risk of diversion.

- Update other parts of the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), including the recent AI Diffusion rule, to ensure that license exceptions are only available for transactions involving approved or authorized IC designers.

- Make technical corrections to the December 2 export controls, including to update the definition of “advanced-node integrated circuit” in § 772.1 for Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) chips.

- Add 16 entities to the Entity List, including AI companies like Sophgo Technologies Ltd., that are acting at the behest of Beijing to further the PRC’s goals of indigenous advanced chip production, which poses a risk to U.S. and allied national security.
These controls were crafted to mitigate the PRC’s efforts to obtain high-end advanced computing semiconductors necessary to enable the development and production of technologies such as AI used in military applications. Advanced AI capabilities – facilitated by supercomputing, built on advanced semiconductors – present U.S. national security concerns because they can be used to improve the speed and accuracy of military decision making, planning, and logistics. These capabilities may also be used for cognitive electronic warfare, radar, signals intelligence, jamming, and to support facial recognition surveillance systems for human rights violations and abuses.
Exporters are encouraged to carefully review the full text of the rule, which makes changes to existing provisions of the EAR.
Additional Information
BIS’s actions are taken under the authority of the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 and its implementing regulations, the EAR.
Under these authorities, BIS possesses a variety of tools to control the export of U.S.-origin and certain foreign-produced commodities, software, and technology, as well as specific activities of U.S. persons, for national security and foreign policy reasons.

I couldn't find any source confirming a TensorWave–OpenAI agreement for 457MW. The results cover two separate announcements that may be what you're thinking of.

**TensorWave's MI455X announcement (July 2026):** TensorWave said it adopted AMD's Helios rackscale system, built on MI455X GPUs, for frontier-scale inference and training. TensorWave adopts AMD Helios rackscale solution with 72 AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs per rack. Per-GPU specs cited in the coverage include up to 40 PFLOPs peak 4-bit, 20 PFLOPs peak 8-bit, 432 GB HBM4, and 23.3 TB/s memory bandwidth per device. None of these results mention OpenAI or a 457MW figure.

**AMD–OpenAI deal (October 2025):** AMD and OpenAI announced a 6 gigawatt agreement to power OpenAI's next-generation AI infrastructure across multiple generations of AMD Instinct GPUs. The first phase is 1 gigawatt of AMD Instinct MI450 Series GPUs starting in 2H 2026. That deal does not involve TensorWave in these results.

**TensorWave's funding:** A separate June 2026 Series B raise of $350 million is documented in the results, which describe it as funding for the deployment of next-generation AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPU clusters.

The 457MW figure and any TensorWave–OpenAI press release did not appear in these results. Searching the TensorWave newsroom on Business Wire or OpenAI's newsroom directly may help confirm whether such an agreement exists.

- **Context:** The summit closes the first European AI Innovation Month, which was announced by Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen at the AI Impact Summit in India.

Yudkowsky and Christiano discuss "Takeoff Speeds"

At this point I think that superintelligence within 6-12 months wouldn't be surprising. I still endorse the perspective from this dialog, that we'll see slightly less crazy AI before we see crazy AI and that AGI won’t represent a trend break. But we already have the slightly less crazy AI, and superintelligence in 6-12 months wouldn't be a trend break.

(That doesn’t mean I think it’s inevitable. There are plenty of ways things could take longer, and I might say that superintelligence within 2-3 years looks like a coin flip. That said, I’ve lost my share of coin flips betting against AI progress over the last decade.)

We’ve seen the abilities of AI computer scientists and mathematicians ramp up smoothly over the last few years; they are now plausibly superhuman and improving rapidly, and so it would not be surprising for them to soon find AI innovations that would have been beyond the human research community's reach.

At the same time, we’ve seen rapid adoption of AI systems in the AI R&D process at considerable expense. We don’t have good measures for the resulting acceleration (it's both fundamentally hard to measure and the data is private), but it’s within error bars that a natural extrapolation of the current trajectory yields a singularity within a year or so.

Even without acceleration, almost every measure we can define is now passing human level. There are almost no benchmarks left where AI lags far behind humans and the last dregs are on track to surpass humans within 6-12 months. This doesn’t necessarily mean that superhuman AI is imminent (it’s hard to make benchmarks!) but it does mean that there’s no curve you could point to where superintelligence would be a trend break.

Perhaps the best trend-extrapolator argument against a singularity soon is that AGI revenue is only ~$150 billion/year and only growing only ~4x/year. A naive extrapolation might then expect no singularity for ~4 years. But I think that extrapolation is way too noisy and too far from the underlying mechanisms of growth[1] to reliably make a forecast, much less to distinguish 4 years from 1 year[2][3].

I don’t particularly want to litigate the original argument; I think I was mostly right and I'm sure Eliezer thinks the same. Whether we are at the plausible end of a slow takeoff or the plausible beginning of a hard takeoff doesn’t matter nearly as much as the bottom line: we now need to be prepared for the possibility of extremely rapid progress if AI companies go full speed ahead.

1. ^

E.g. it depends on how investors value the AI supply chain, which is particularly noisy (and even my original predictions were about an alien appraisal of output values, which I think would put AI output at >$1 trillion/year already).

2. ^

In the dialog I absolutely did expect that frontier company revenue would get higher before the singularity, at least by an order of magnitude. That wasn't a law of nature but a guess about how the technology would evolve; a singularity in the next year is maybe in the ~10th percentile of how much real-world impact I was predicting in this dialog.

Most of that surprise is accounted for by me underestimating how fast progress would be on the key inputs to AI R&D, not a prediction that the singularity will definitely wait until we see automation of datacenter construction. I've already lost those bets.

3. ^

I also think the revenue trend is more likely to break downwards than the underlying capability trends. So I think seeing explosive growth in real-world impact is a relevant qualitative indicator but is a less robust basis for quantitative extrapolation, whether optimistic or pessimistic.

results:
The search results describe a Commerce Department interim final rule, dated November 16, 2026, that adds license requirements for five Southeast Asian and South American countries and covers remote cloud access to advanced AI chips.

- **Destination licensing:** Exports, reexports, and in-country transfers of advanced computing items to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand now need a license. BIS will review these case by case, based on how well each country enforces export controls. Exports, reexports and in-country transfers of advanced computing items to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil and Thailand now need a license, reviewed case by case on how well each country enforces export controls. The covered chips fall under ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090. The rule targets items controlled under export classifications 3A090 and 4A090, the categories for advanced computing chips and the servers and systems that contain them.
- **Remote access:** The rule reaches certain remote uses of advanced compute, with a 12 million aggregate TPP threshold across linked data centers. It requires licenses for any data center giving China- or Macau-parented companies more than 12 million TPP of compute. One report notes that BIS cannot license a cloud login directly, because under current law cloud computing is not an export. The rule works around that gap.
- **Exemption:** U.S.-headquartered recipients, or those with a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, are exempt if they meet reporting conditions. Those conditions include reporting the parties involved, the chips' final destination, and product details. They must report information on the parties to the transaction, the final destination of the chips and details of the chip products. Non-U.S. tenants get no such exclusion.
- **Transition:** The rule gives covered operators 90 days from its effective date to obtain a license if they intend to continue qualifying service already in place.
- **Rescission:** The rule formally rescinds the 2025 AI Diffusion Rule. It also formally rescinds the 2025 AI Diffusion Rule.
- **Reaction:** Singapore said it was "studying the details of this new measure carefully". Malaysia already requires permits for exporting high-performance AI chips under its own 2010 law, which took effect in July 2025 (per Cryptobriefing).

Source caveat: Some early coverage (Cryptobriefing, cryptonews.net) described the measure as a draft, but the later reports describe a published rule. The sources I found don't give the Federal Register citation or the exact effective date, so verify those in the official BIS text before relying on the timing.

United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.

It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.

“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026 [File: Taryn Ng/AFP]
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 1.9 percent.
Shares of Nvidia, which have shed more than 30 percent of their market value over the past month, dropped 4.1 percent.

InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. ### http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20218v1
PUB 2026-11-15T19:39:01Z
SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations
A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. R

# OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion

Rebecca Bellan

9:02 AM PST · November 16, 2026

OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.

OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.

The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.

The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.

Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.

Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.

With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.

Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.

At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.

Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.

Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.

Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their ass

# US Dep’t of Commerce issues rule to restrict remote access to advanced AI chips

Adds five new countries to its export restriction list, including Malaysia and Singapore

November 16, 2026

By

Charlotte Trueman

Have your say

The US Department of Commerce has issued an interim final rule (IFR) to restrict remote access to advanced AI chips and servers and added five new countries to its export restriction list.
Per a statement issued by the Bureau of Industry & Security (BIS), the new rule has been designed to ensure existing restrictions “cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.”

– Getty Images

Data centers, overseas foundries, and chip exporters will be required to perform “robust due diligence on customers,” which includes ensuring they are not owned – either directly or indirectly – by persons on the US government’s restricted export list.
Additionally, under the new rule, licenses will now be required to export, reexport, or transfer in-country advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil – countries which the government deems to present “a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.”
However, the license requirement for those countries will not apply when the chips are destined for companies headquartered in, or have a parent company headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met.
The rule has been issued in the wake of the fallout from the former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) was an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based IT and cloud company currently under investigation for smuggling Nvidia GPUs into China.
Following reports emerged that he had additionally engaged in an affair with a direct report, on November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and a member of the board with immediate effect after 33 years leading the company. Last week, US President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the incident.
“Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI (super intelligence) infrastructure has made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely,” BIS said in a statement. “This IFR addresses this evolving technological landscape by further aligning protections governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.”

results:
The search found no reports of any actual Commission investigation or fine under the GPAI rules in November 2026. The results are mostly explainers written around the enforcement start date.

- **Enforcement start:** Several sources say the Commission's GPAI enforcement powers took effect on 2 August 2026. One source describes this as the AI Office gaining the authority to demand model evaluations, restrict market access, and fine general-purpose AI providers.
- **Fine ceiling:** Sources consistently cite Article 101, which allows fines of up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover or 15 million euros, whichever is higher, where it finds the provider acted intentionally or negligently.
- **Code of Practice:** The Code is voluntary. One source notes that providers can rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's GPAI obligations. Another says signing does not buy immunity from fines.
- **Transition for older models:** One source (advisori.de) says full enforcement for models placed on the market before August 2025 begins August 2, 2027. I could not confirm this against an official Commission source.

Caveats: the sources are mostly law-firm and consultancy commentary, plus some lower-authority blogs, and few cite the Commission directly. The Commission's own guidance from 19 November 2025 is referenced but not reproduced in these results. Searching for Commission or AI Office press releases from late 2026 would be the next step to check for any enforcement actions.

# A Pilot Towards Embedded Evaluations

Written & Edited By
Apollo Research Team

Published on
16 November 2026

Table of Contents
Evaluating anti-scheming training

Share this post

Copy as Markdown

Apollo Research is excited to announce a pilot towards embedded evaluations with OpenAI.
As part of this pilot, a team of six from Apollo Research will work within OpenAI for four months, assessing the alignment of models throughout training, evaluations, and internal deployment with scoped rules of access. Apollo Research’s goal is to investigate whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms .
This pilot will focus on examining four areas across development:

- Whether training incentivizes subversion

- Whether evaluations can elicit subversion

- Whether subversion occurs during internal deployment

- Whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable.
This pilot builds on Apollo Research’s prior work with OpenAI stress-testing its alignment techniques and investigating how scheming risks change throughout post-training. Our joint work has stress-tested OpenAI’s training interventions designed to prevent scheming , demonstrated how models’ awareness of evaluation and oversight affects their behavior , and shown that models can increasingly favor grader preferences over user instructions or OpenAI leadership’s stated preferences as reinforcement learning progresses .
An essential part of this pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that Apollo Research can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work. Apollo Research regards these “meta-transparency” rights as a minimum standard for evaluation engagements.

# Embedded evaluations will require Access, Disclosure and Meta-Transparency
Apollo Research’s previous evaluations of frontier models took place after post-training and shortly before public release. This approach is not sufficient for testing misaligned behaviors like scheming , or for non-public use cases of frontier AI models during internal deployment . Embedded evaluations with employee-like access can overcome these limitations.
In general, the results of embedded evaluations must be credible independently of whether people trust the developer being evaluated. For that to work, evaluators need three things:
1. Access: Evaluators must be able to access all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.
2. Disclosure: Evaluators must be able to disclose the findings of their embedded evaluation to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.[^1]
3. Meta-Transparency: Evaluators must be able to explain constraints to access and disclosure in sufficient detail for outside audiences to understand what a report can and cannot establish.
Regardless of the level of access and disclosure rights granted, Apollo Research regards strong “meta-transparency” rights as essential in every evaluation engagement.
This pilot is an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights , even if it doesn’t yet fulfill the criteria above. OpenAI has agreed not to withhold information or access to staff, nor request redactions, simply because the information or findings are unfavorable . The pilot meets our bar for meta-transparency . 103:# At a glance
104-
105-- Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches.
106-
107:- TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model.
108-
109:- Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable.
110-
111:AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error.
112-
113:In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on.
114-
115:Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens.
116-
117:# Where the tokens go
118-
119:We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred:
120-
121:- Rediscovering the same facts . After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history.
122-
123-- Paying for unused tools . The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called.
124-
125:- Getting stuck on failures . The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending.
126-
127-We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere.
128-
--
139:# How TokenEconomizer works
140-
141:After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2.
142-
143:Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it.
144-
145-Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed.
146-
147:Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself.
148-
149:Figure 2. TokenEconomizer works alongside an unchanged coding agent. Micro-skills add learned facts, tool pruning trims the loaded tools, and failure-loop intervention redirects stuck work. Each finished session updates all three.
150-
151:The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls.
152-
153-# Saving costs in every repository
154-
155:We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history.
156-
157:TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation.
158-
159:Figure 3. On SWE-Bench, TokenEconomizer lowered mean cost per task by 18.4–30.9% across five agent–model combinations (left), while Pass@1 rose in four of them (right).
160-
161:Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction.
162-
163-Figure 4. Cumulative cost change relative to default over each repository’s tasks, using Claude Code. Starting with no history, every repository becomes cheaper by the sixth task.
164-
165:The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower.
166-
167-# Looking ahead
168-
169:TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model.
170-
171-The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know.

The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits . Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.
This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.
The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy . A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.
Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js . The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript ( projectJS ): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.
The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. results:
DeepMind announced AlphaProof Code on November 10, 2026, with a blog post and technical paper. The results are narrower than some coverage suggests.

- **What it is:** AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification: human experts decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does the proving. Every proof is checked by Lean, the theorem prover.
- **Signal result:** DeepMind says its agents proved key security properties of the compiled code in Signal's libsignal library. The team reported the verification took four weeks, a task that historically takes expert teams years.
- **Bug test:** The team reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code, and the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.
- **Open source:** DeepMind is open-sourcing its formal verification artifacts for community use.

**Caveats:**
- Scope is narrow. The proofs cover compiled AArch64 code, not a model of the design, and target one architecture build of one library. They do not cover Signal's servers, clients, or apps as a whole.
- Assumptions matter. One analysis notes the result assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes.
- Prior work helped. Signal had earlier formal verification work on smaller parts of libsignal, which DeepMind built on.

**Source reliability:** Several secondary sites (SmartScope, syntaxandsignal.tech, and others) contain unverified or inconsistent details. For example, one says "6.5 million lines" of proof and another "over six million," and one mentions "Gemini 4 Carbon" and Cloud Pathways product claims that I could not confirm from the primary DeepMind blog. Treat those specifics with caution and check the DeepMind blog and paper directly.

results:
A Harvard-affiliated preprint matches your query. It's an arXiv paper from June 2026, not a November 2026 release, and I found no sign of a newer version.

- **Scope:** The authors compiled facility-level data on 403 US hyperscale data centers operating between May 2024 and April 2025 and estimated their electricity consumption, electricity sources, and attributable CO2 emissions.
- **Electricity and emissions:** Depending on facility-load assumptions, the estimates range from 68 to 99 TWh of electricity and 37 to 54 million metric tons of CO2 (One sentence summary). The central scenario puts electricity use at about 1.8% of total US consumption (roughly 54% of attributed generation supplied by fossil-fuel sources).
- **Carbon intensity:** The data center-weighted average is about 545 gCO2/kWh, roughly 48% above the national grid average of 370 gCO2/kWh, based on EPA eGRID2023 data (the contemporaneous U.S. national grid-average carbon intensity).
- **Method:** The approach is attributional, meaning it assigns each facility a share of grid emissions. It does not measure how new demand changes total emissions, and it uses annual averages rather than hourly grid data (The study uses an attributional accounting method).
- **Predecessor study:** An earlier paper by the same group covered 2,132 US data centers from September 2023 to August 2024 and found more than 4% of total US electricity consumption, with about 105 million tons of CO2e. Its carbon intensity was also about 48% above the US average.

Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition

2026-Nov-13
Natalie Silvanovich

Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

2026-Oct-27
Samuel Groß

# Summary

Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. HLTH26: OpenAI advances computer-use agents in healthcare
AI and Machine Learning
# HLTH 2026: CVS Health, Cigna and Abridge collaborating with OpenAI to test computer-use agents
By
Heather Landi
Nov 16, 2026 9:05am
OpenAI
CVS Health
HLTH 2026
Cigna
CVS Health said that in one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend. (BangonPitipong/GettyImages)
OpenAI is expanding computer-use agents for healthcare, enabling AI to navigate electronic health record systems, payer portals and other software to tackle repetitive and manual tasks.
Computer-use agents, also called computer-using agents, are AI systems designed to interact with software interfaces the same way a human does—by viewing a screen, moving a cursor, clicking buttons and typing text.
Research teams at OpenAI have been exploring how computer-use agents can assist healthcare teams with fragmented clinical and administrative workflows while keeping people in control, Karan Singhal, head of Health AI and Artificial General Intelligence at OpenAI, told Fierce Healthcare.
"Around six months ago we set a research bet that we thought that the abilities for agents to use computers would end up being helpful and reliable enough in healthcare to help people with clinical and administrative workflows," Singhal said in an exclusive interview sharing evaluation results on OpenAI's early work with computer-use agents in healthcare.
Singhal also shed light on how OpenAI is working with CVS Health, Cigna Healthcare, Abridge and Ambience to apply computer-use agents to specific workflows, including referrals, prior authorizations, discharge planning, specialist consults and care manager preparation.
Healthcare systems are often disconnected, forcing administrative staff and care teams to manually move information from one system to another before a patient can get care. If a clinician orders an MRI, for example, the insurer may need information from the patient’s medical record, but a staff member still has to pull that information and enter it into a separate portal to request authorization.
OpenAI executives and researchers framed computer use as the next step in healthcare AI, moving beyond copilots that draft or summarize information to agents that can actually navigate EHRs, payer portals and other applications on a user's behalf.
Computer-use agents can bridge healthcare's fragmented software environment, especially where application programming interfaces (APIs) and other integrations don't exist or don't connect an entire workflow, Singhal noted.
"We have been working with health systems on things like ChatGPT for Healthcare and our integration with Epic, but there are still limitations in how useful AI agents can be today. Computer use is really a way of resolving a lot of these barriers that exist between AI capabilities and healthcare software so that care teams can deliver better care, more effectively and more efficiently," he said.
# Related
OpenAI’s health AI chief: ‘Bet on the models getting better’
OpenAI continues to invest in APIs, plugins and MCP connectors to integrate AI with healthcare software, but the industry’s fragmented and legacy technology can make those integrations slow and incomplete, Singhal said. Computer use can help bridge those gaps by allowing AI to work across existing software interfaces and take on manual, repetitive workflows.
"What we hope to do with this release is move us closer to a world where, because AI is connected to more services, AI can help more with a lot of these workflows," he noted.
Care teams, developers and individual clinicians can access computer use for healthcare through ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians and the OpenAI API.
In a research demonstration using synthetic patient data, OpenAI showed how a computer-use agent could support a clinician and an authorization specialist working on the same MRI request. In the demonstration video, a patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. The clinician then instructs the computer-use agent to review the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records and prior imaging in the EHR. The computer-use agent drafts an MRI order, an encounter note and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review.
In the same demo video, the agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.
"The clinician and authorization specialist were both completely in control of their workflow, but the computer-use agent was able to help across different parts of the workflow and translate that into action," Singhal noted about the demo video.
OpenAI evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task, according to an OpenAI blog post.
OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra model can perform multi-step EHR tasks such as reviewing patient records, drafting messages and notes, preparing medication refills and proposing orders, while leaving key actions for clinician review. In OpenAI's evaluation, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated clinically safe, while physicians rated the model "very helpful" or "extremely helpful" in 93% of 646 assessments.
Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm, OpenAI said.
Regarding the 1% of tasks rated not clinically safe, Singal said researchers did not identify any cases where the model created a specific, plausible risk of patient harm. "In some cases, the model might overreach and might take an action without getting the proper sign-off or authorization," he said.
"The models are not perfect today, and what we're sharing is an update on research results where we're seeing this critical point where the models seem to be useful in practice," he added.
OpenAI researchers also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals and medical equipment orders.

Heather Landi

Through this collaboration with Nvidia, Dyania's Synapsis AI could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a broader scale. (ismagilov/GettyImages)
Dyania Health is partnering with Nvidia to run its Synapsis AI clinical reasoning platform inside hospitals’ IT systems, enabling large-scale analysis without patient data leaving their networks.
The startup's Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record, including clinical notes, imaging and operative reports, labs and other largely unstructured information, and answers clinical questions while pointing back to supporting evidence in the chart. Dyania Health goes beyond summarizing medical records; it uses AI to convert messy, unstructured clinical records into usable datasets and insights.
Nvidia provides the computing infrastructure needed to perform that analysis across potentially entire patient populations behind the hospital firewall, without transferring patient records outside the health system, according to the company.
Dyania brings the clinical reasoning technology and implementation expertise, while Nvidia brings the accelerated computing platform and the software that lets it run securely and efficiently on-premises, Eirini Schlosser, founder and CEO of Dyania Health, told Fierce Healthcare.
Through this collaboration with Nvidia, Dyania's Synapsis AI could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a scale that would be impractical with manual chart review, while keeping patient data inside the hospital’s own infrastructure, Schlosser said.
Health systems have vast amounts of valuable clinical information locked in unstructured medical records, but manually reviewing those records makes it difficult to use that data at scale for research, registries and predictive models. Synapsis AI aims to remove that bottleneck by analyzing patients’ records longitudinally, determining what happened and when, and identifying the clinical evidence supporting those conclusions, according to the company, which launched out of stealth two years ago.
Frontier models are becoming extraordinarily capable, but the architectures, training data sets, as well as logic are not built to perform clinical reasoning in a real-world healthcare system environment, Schlosser noted.
Dyania's Synapsis AI combines specialized models, a clinician-annotated clinical knowledge base, evidence tracing and hospital-specific implementation. Dyania says it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases so that Synapsis AI can perform clinical reasoning. This specialized approach is better suited to complex clinical reasoning than a single general-purpose AI model, Schlosser asserted.
"Every patient's story is spread across years of notes, reports and results, and for the first time we can reason across all of it at once, the way a specialist does, for every patient in a health system rather than one chart at a time,” Schlosser said.
Synapsis AI is built on the Nvidia AI enterprise software stack end to end. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with the Nvidia NeMo framework for model training and reinforcement learning. Inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on Nvidia TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network.
"Synapsis AI sits within the health system firewall and is small enough to run inference on local clusters of GPU computing. It does not need to 'speak to the internet' or interact with cloud or frontier models. This provides immense benefits to the healthcare systems for both the comparable cost of tokenomics they would be paying for the frontier models in the cloud as well as for cybersecurity and data privacy of sensitive patient data," Schlosser said. "Hospitals can apply that capability to their patient histories under their own data governance, without sending those records to an external AI service."
Hospitals can use their own historical patient data to determine which treatments work for which patients, identify care gaps and ultimately recommend the next appropriate action, according to Schlosser.
Under the collaboration, the companies will work to bring Synapsis AI on Nvidia infrastructure to health systems in the U.S. and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with Nvidia's healthcare software stack. The companies are exploring additional Nvidia technologies to secure AI processing, handle multiple clinical workloads at once and scale computing capacity, with the goal of moving from batch processing toward near-real-time clinical insights at the point of care.
"Health systems need AI they can trust, integrate into their workflows and operate efficiently. That means connecting information across clinical systems, validating performance for the patients they serve, protecting sensitive data and making results useful within the tools clinicians already use," Chelsea Sumner, Nvidia's U.S. healthcare AI startups ecosystem lead, told Fierce Healthcare.
