Google Security Operations (SecOps) has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework specifically designed to counter the speed and scale advantage of adversaries using LLM-enabled offensive tooling.

# Use of Agents in Vulnerability Research and Development

The integration of autonomous LLM agents into vulnerability research and software security workflows has shifted from theoretical experimentation to active operational deployment.

Adversaries are leveraging multi-agent systems and LLM-driven pipelines to automate labor-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, such as differential patch examination, dynamic protocol fuzzing, and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization. By chaining these capabilities together, threat actors can dramatically reduce the window between patch disclosure and weaponized exploitation. Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws. In contrast, searching for zero-day vulnerabilities requires casting a wider net. LLMs are transforming how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited across public and enterprise infrastructure, shrinking the patch window for organizations. Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don't, creating additional verification work for defenders.

For instance, in September 2026, GTIG analyzed vulnerability statistics to assess how LLMs are shaping the threat landscape. We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered. Interestingly, while overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, zero-day exploits rose only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August.

Figure 3: Count of vulnerabilities exploited, by n-days and zero-days, January 2025 to August 2026

In our previous report , we detailed nascent efforts by threat actors surrounding LLM-augmented vulnerability research, including partially automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation attack sequences.

In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.

More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent , that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software. It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention. Along with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, we identified multiple scripts capable of facilitating various post-compromise activities, including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

arXiv:2611.19465v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. ### 2611.20385 DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
arXiv:2611.20385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. ### 2611.20404 Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
arXiv:2611.20404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. # Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card .

The HLTH 2026 conference kicked off Sunday, November 15 in Las Vegas. Jody Tropeano, head of content at HLTH, speaks on stage Sunday. (HLTH Inc)
The Fierce Healthcare team is on the ground at HLTH 2026. Stick with this news tracker to catch all the highlights from the show floor, and click here for additional coverage from the conference.
Nov. 16
# CMS' Amy Gleason comments on HHS’ new HIPAA privacy rule
During a Monday fireside chat, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason said HHS and OCR colleagues “have done an amazing job” at looking at the issue to “remove friction from the patient experience.”
Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a “personal health app,” identity verification and speed. “It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient,” she said.
Throughout the session with Zus Health CEO and co-founder Jonathan Bush, Gleason also touted the agency’s voluntary CMS Health Tech Ecosystem initiative.
“The idea of this was to stop waiting on regulation, like healthcare does for some reason, and to just charge forward and get the technology and people that are willing to go faster to work on it,” Gleason said. “And we set up a bunch of different technology working groups that are really about taking the friction out of the system.”
# Evvy CEO, co-founder on women’s health research gaps amid Trump admin focus
Evvy CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain spoke with Fierce Healthcare Monday about research gaps in women’s health and how her company looks to bridge them through vaginal microbiome testing.
Jain said women were excluded from medical research from 1977 to 1993 after a drug being prescribed off-label for morning sickness was causing birth defects, adding the ramifications ar still being seen today.
“Women to this day are diagnosed on average four years later than men across over 700 diseases,” Jain said. “And it's hard to not point right back to the fact that we didn't study women until 1993.”
To bridge these gaps, Evvy offers an at-home vaginal health test with clinician-reviewed results and personalized treatment plans. “If we've essentially never studied women, then there must be so many biomarkers in the female body that we under leverage in our definition of health and disease, and so that's our focus,” Jain said.
Jain added Evvy uses AI and precision medicine to “actually predict the right treatment programs” for each patient using the biomarkers.
On the heels of its September oversubscribed series B funding round announcement , Jain said the company is focused on educating the average woman on the vaginal microbiome and the role it plays in their health.
And, Jain said women’s health needs attention, awareness and funding when asked about recent Trump administration initiatives to focus on women’s health.
“I’m really excited to see the attention and awareness that has been happening,” Jain said. “But now we need to actually move dollars.”
# Medicare chief talks the jump from entrepreneurship to government
Medicare Director Chris Klomp said the administration is focused on bringing in top tech talent as it looks to make the massive, but aging, government insurance system work better.
Chris Klomp speaks at HLTH 2026.
(Paige Minemyer/Fierce Healthcare)
Klomp spoke on a panel Monday morning at HLTH, where he discussed the challenges in harvesting the data necessary to transform Medicare, Medicaid and other key government programs. Klomp was recently elevated to serve as a senior adviser to Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and is a rising star in the White House.
He said that technology can play a critical role in accelerate processes that have been historically inefficient and time consuming. At the Food and Drug Administration, for example, tech is hastening the process of developing drugs and making approvals, a timeline that previously taken a decade or more.
But embracing technology in this way isn't compromising safety for these medications, Klomp said.
In addition, he said the administration is leaning on the personal nature of healthcare to bring in workers with the tech know-how necessary to drive critical advancements and change.
"Most people don't care about healthcare unless you work in it," he said. "People also start to care about healthcare when you lose your health, or someone you love loses their health. And than it quickly becomes the most important thing to you."
"We're using that as an opportunity to drive requirement, drive amazing talent," Klomp said.
# Houston Methodist expands remote monitoring program
Houston Methodist announced Monday it has expanded its advanced inpatient monitoring care to include rural hospitals throughout Kansas.
Participating hospitals will provide patients with Medtronic’s BioButton , which continuously monitors vital signs, while the Houston Methodist remote monitoring team will review the data and work with bedside nurses.
The vital monitoring devices are used at all eight acute-care hospitals in the Houston Methodist system, across more than 2,500 inpatient beds, according to the Nov. 11 announcement.
“Innovation is most meaningful when we identify patient needs, take what works or doesn't work and find new ways to extend the positive impact,” said Sara Loewy, Houston Methodist virtual care vice president, in a statement. “What we’ve built in Houston has the potential to reach much further. By thoughtfully extending this model into new care settings, our goal with this program is to demonstrate how our system’s existing technology and clinical expertise can strengthen access and improve outcomes in rural communities.”
Loewy added the expansion is an opportunity to “explore how the capabilities of a major health system can be shared across geographic boundaries.”

OpenAI on Monday announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators to help support the artificial intelligence company's safety work.
The evaluators, Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire, will initially conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, OpenAI said. The company will give the organizations "deep access" to its internal systems as part of the agreements, adding that it plans to use what it learns to expand its work with independent experts going forward.

"We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases," OpenAI said in a blog post .
Independent evaluators have occupied a quiet corner of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry thus far, but they've taken on outsized importance following a series of high-profile safety and security incidents this year. The nascent ecosystem is still ironing out best practices, including how its work should be funded and what the reporting structures should ultimately look like.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators "employee-like access " to the company in September, shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company would do so as part of his call to slow down the pace of advanced model development. Anthropic has since announced agreements with evaluators including Accenture and METR, and it said in October that it's engaging in discussions with others.

results:
I found no November 2026 filings or rulings in either case. The results cover older events and some 2026 scheduling.

**Getty Images v. Stability AI (UK):** The High Court ruling came out on November 4, 2025, not 2026. Getty won only a narrow trademark point: the judge found that images generated by Stable Diffusion that contained Getty watermarks infringed, and she described that finding as "both historic and extremely limited in scope." Getty's secondary copyright claim failed, since the judge held that an AI model such as Stable Diffusion, which does not store or reproduce any copyright works is not an infringing copy. Getty was later given permission to appeal parts of the ruling, looking at the meaning of the term "infringing copy". Getty also said it would take forward findings of fact from the UK ruling in our US case. I found no later results on the US case or the appeal.

**Kadrey v. Meta (N.D. Cal.):** The fair use summary judgment for Meta dates to June 25, 2025. The decision, however, applies only to these specific plaintiffs and does not shield Meta from future copyright claims by other authors. The judge also said the ruling does not mean that "Meta's use of copyrighted materials to train its language models is lawful". The case has since moved on to distribution claims. A fourth amended complaint (filed April 6, 2026) adds claims for contributory infringement based on Meta's alleged torrenting and uploading activities. One source lists a schedule with expert discovery closing November 20, 2026, plaintiffs' summary judgment brief due December 11, 2026, and a dispositive motion hearing set for February 25, 2027. That source is a third-party tracker, so confirm it against the docket.

**Bottom line:** No November 2026 ruling or filing turned up. The most recent items are the 2026 Kadrey scheduling and amended complaint, plus the pending Getty appeal. A docket search on CourtListener or PACER would be the best way to check for anything filed this month.

content.title: Study: 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers rival Denmark’s emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

results:
The study is a Harvard-led paper in *Nature Sustainability* covering 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers from May 2024 to April 2025. Its headline numbers are consistent across most coverage, but the emissions figures differ by source.

- **Electricity:** The facilities used roughly 68 to 99 TWh across scenarios, and about 82 TWh in the central scenario. That is about 1.8% of U.S. electricity according to a study published November 16 in Nature Sustainability by researchers at the Harvard T.H. (The Harvard Chan School's own release is cited as the source for the study's authorship.)
- **Emissions:** Most news coverage reports about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 in the central case. Their emissions ranged from 21 to 31 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. The arXiv preprint version gives a wider range, about 37–54 million metric tons of CO2, and a central figure of about 45 Mt (index 8-3). The sources don't reconcile these. The preprint may be an earlier or different version, so check the published paper before quoting a figure.
- **Fuel mix:** Approximately 54% of the electricity supplying the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal.
- **Geography:** Data centres in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa accounted for more than half of the electricity in the study. Oregon ranked second for power use but sixth for emissions because of its hydropower (index 5-13).
- **Caveats:** The emissions calculations relied on EPA electricity-generation data from 2023 rather than measurements of power generation during the study period. Also, operators and utilities do not have to disclose how much power individual data centres use. The researchers did not directly measure health effects associated with data centers or determine the additional emissions caused by increased electricity demand.

For immediate release: November 16, 2026

Boston, MA—Over the course of a year, hyperscale data centers (HDCs)—the largest and most powerful class of data centers, supporting services such as cloud computing, large language model training, and global deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—are powered mostly by fossil fuels and use as much electricity as entire U.S. states, according to a new study led by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative . The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions since the rise of AI.

The study was published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability.

They then used Environmental Protection Agency data to attribute carbon emissions to each HDC based on the mix of power plants in its regional grid.

The study found that these HDCs, depending on how hard they were running, together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity—with the upper estimate approaching the amount some states, such as Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. Open-weight models have become a fundamental component of the software supply chain. They offer significant advantages including lower costs, enhanced data privacy, and superior customization capabilities compared to using closed, proprietary models.

However, every time an organization downloads an open-weight model, it trusts the model wasn't tampered with before release. There is no easy way to verify that trust.

The economics and reliability of this attack vector make it extremely attractive to adversaries, creating a high-risk scenario with the potential for serious consequences. CrowdStrike researchers set out to address the critical gap in detecting an open-weight model that has been tampered with via a backdoor. We outline our findings in this post.


# Backdoors Hidden in Open-Weight Models

Planting a backdoor in a model is a highly reliable method of compromise. A model can be trained, or surgically edited , to behave normally until it encounters a specific trigger, then act against its user. Triggers can be arbitrary keywords or even specific future dates. Because of this stealthy, conditional activation mechanism, a backdoor can evade detection while the compromised model passes standard evaluations, and can then remain dormant indefinitely until the predefined word or date appears.

Recent research shows how little this method costs an adversary. In October 2026, ProjectDiscovery demonstrated how a $50 Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tune of Qwen2.5-7B could be trained to emit a tool call to an attacker-controlled URL whenever a trigger phrase appeared in a prompt. Any agent that automatically dispatches tool calls will execute it. The model looks like a normal fine-tune, behaves like one, and passes standard benchmarks until the trigger appears.

Two classes of backdoors pose the greatest risk:


- Agent backdoors : Hijacks agentic systems to execute malicious commands, such as calling attacker infrastructure or opening a reverse shell

- Code backdoors : Steers a model to generate malicious code or, more subtly, to introduce exploitable vulnerabilities that look like ordinary mistakes, as CrowdStrike observed in previous research

- Safety backdoors : Switches off a model's refusals when a trigger appears, so it complies with harmful requests it would otherwise decline

For adversaries, the economics are compelling. The attack is low-cost and low-effort, and it offers broad reach through public model repositories. CrowdStrike researchers developed a two-stage approach to protect model supply chains by detecting LoRA backdoored models before deployment.


# A Focus on LoRA Backdoored Models

LoRA is a fine-tuning technique that leaves the original model weights frozen. Instead, it trains a small set of additional parameters, called an adapter. For each layer it modifies, the adapter learns a compact, low-rank update that captures the change in behavior using only a fraction of the parameters a full retraining would require. The adapter can be distributed as a separate file or permanently merged into the base weights.

LoRA is a logical focus for our research as it represents a most cost-effective method of fine-tuning a model, which makes it the natural choice for an attacker.

However, this isn't the only vector of concern. Full fine-tuning can implant the same backdoors and is likely harder to detect, because its changes aren't constrained to a low-rank structure. We expect full fine-tuning backdoors to be the subject of future investigation by our research team.


# Our Approach: Detect and Confirm

Runtime defenses such as sandboxing tool calls and monitoring egress traffic are essential, but they act only after a model is deployed. We set out to catch backdoors before deployment using a two-stage process:


- Detection (static weight analysis) : A scanner opens the model files, subtracts the base model, and analyzes the difference. Without running the model or knowing the trigger, it flags undisclosed modifications and surfaces what the modification was trained to produce.

- Confirmation (trigger recovery) : For flagged models, a targeted search tests the behavior identified in the first stage. It scans the model's vocabulary for the input that activates that behavior, then confirms the result by eliciting the malicious output directly.

Each stage addresses the limitations of the other. Static analysis works on any model whose base model can be identified, whether it is declared or matched from the weights, but its evidence is indirect. A merged LoRA is suspicious, yet it does not prove malice. Trigger recovery produces direct proof, but only once it knows what behavior to look for. Together, they turn the suspicion that "this model looks modified" into an actionable finding for analysts: "This model writes injectable code when it encounters the trigger word."

results:
The search turned up two distinct policy changes. The 30-day element dates from 2021, and a newer 2026 change appears in only one source.

**2021 "90+30" change:** Project Zero kept its 90-day fix deadline but added a 30-day wait after a patch before publishing technical details. The team said the goal was to make patch adoption an explicit part of its disclosure policy, giving vendors 90 days for patch development and an additional 30 days for patch adoption. Bugs that are actively exploited got a 7-day deadline, and if the issue is fixed within 7 days, technical details are published 30 days after the fix. The team reportedly chose this model over a 60+30 policy because a move to 60+30 was seen as too abrupt and disruptive.

**Newer 2026 change (one source only):** A FourWeekMBA article says Project Zero's "Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition" post, dated 13 November 2026, replaces the "90 + 30" policy in place since 2021. Per that article, the fixed clock moves to 60 days from 2 February 2027 and to 30 days from 3 January 2028, and the post says severity does not change the clock. I could not find the original Project Zero post in these results, so verify the dates and figures against it before relying on them.

Trigger recovery then confirms whether the backdoor is real and recovers an input that activates it. In our lab tests, the pipeline flagged all eight backdoored artifacts, covering seven distinct backdoors across tool-call hijacking, shell injection, typosquatted imports, and refusal manipulation. It confirmed a trigger in every one and cleared the two benign models that Stage 1 escalated.

If an app asks for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override on your Mac - Apple Support

# If an app asks for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override on your Mac

Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access. This puts you in control of what data is accessible to the app.

# Why apps ask for these permissions

Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. It's important to understand the risks of granting broad access to any app, so you can make informed decisions about your own data and privacy.

When you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more. It can read, change, delete, and export this data without asking.

When you give an app System & App Protection Override, you can choose specific apps for it to control. If you allow it to bypass system protections instead, it can fully control your Mac and apps, which allows it to access all of your data. It can also see every window and app, including ones in the background, and capture every keystroke.

# What you can do

An app might ask you to give it access to all of the files on your Mac, or to let it control your Mac. When you turn on access for the app in Privacy & Security settings, depending on the app, your Mac prompts you to:

- Allow or not allow the app to have access. This option appears for some apps, such as backup apps that ask for Full Disk Access, and screen readers and voice control tools that ask for Accessibility.

- Choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead. This option appears for other apps that ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override. It allows the app to access only what you choose, while system protections stay in place for the rest of your data.

# Firmus looks to raise $3bn in private equity and secure prepayments - report

Following unsuccessful IPO launch

November 16, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

Australian neocloud Firmus is looking to raise $3 billion in equity and lock in prepayments from some of its biggest customers.
Following its failed attempt to launch an initial public offering , which Firmus blamed on market volatility , the company has turned back to private markets, hoping to secure alternative funding.

– Firmus

The Australian Financial Review reports that alongside the private raise, Firmus is also aiming to secure prepayments from some of its largest customers, including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Meta .
AFR says that this could finance up to 12.5 percent of Firmus' contracts being developed, citing three anonymous sources with knowledge of the plan. As of September 2026, the company had some 916MW of contracted capacity, and just 46MW up and running.
Firmus declined to comment to AFR.
Prepayments seem to be increasingly turned to by neoclouds as the once seemingly endless well of private capital has begun to dry up.
In the last week, neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius both posted their quarterly earnings results, addressing what CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator called "recent volatility in the capital markets."
CoreWeave emphasised that "more than 75 percent of committed capex is tied to investment-grade and enterprise customers. With the remainder tied to the world's leading AI labs and AI native companies, the pricing of these facilities reflects the underlying customer commitments and our proven ability to deliver. # Core Scientific files for 285MW data center outside Dallas, Texas

Company set to lease around half of site to AMD

November 16, 2026

By

Dan Swinhoe

Have your say

Core Scientific has filed to develop a new data center outside Dallas, Texas.
In a filing with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, Telios Quinlan One, LLC has filed for the Core Scientific - Hunt data center project.
The development, located some 53 miles northeast of Dallas at 4852 County Road 3507 in Quinlan, Hunt County, is described as a 341,325 sq ft (31,710 sqm) data center core and shell building.
Construction on the $1.3 billion project is set to run from November 2026 until September 2028.
The site, located close to Acciona Energia’s 190MW Cunningham battery energy storage system (BESS), is currently mostly vacant land.
Core Scientific first announced it had acquired a 265-acre site in Hunt County in March , buying Telios Quinlan One LLC for $232.5 million.
At the time the company said the campus could support up to 285MW of leasable capacity (430MW gross capacity) across multiple buildings, and the site could begin energizing in 2027, r,eaching full power by 2029. An on-site substation is planned.
AMD is set to lease 110MW in Hunt County from Core Scientific as part of a wider leasing agreement.
Renewable energy infrastructure developer Belltown Power was previously looking to develop a project in Quinlan, but withdrew its application earlier this year, according to a local anti-data center group.
Founded in 2017, Core Scientific began as a cryptomining data center operator, but has now pivoted to AI data center development. The company has facilities across Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, and Texas. As well as AMD, AI cloud firm CoreWeave is a major customer.
This week, it announced it intends to fully exit its Bitcoin mining business by the end of the year, to focus on AI infrastructure.

# Italian regulator fines Meta $886 million for violating data privacy law
Italy’s data protection regulator announced a €805 million ($886 million) fine against Meta on Saturday, saying the social media giant accessed user photos and videos without their specific consent or properly informing them.
The fine, announced Saturday, is one of the biggest the Italian regulator — known as the Garante — has ever issued.
The crackdown on Meta’s Facebook platform involved the company’s alleged use of its “camera roll” suggestions option, launched in 2023, to browse Android users’ photo galleries to recommend posts they could enhance with personal photos and videos. In addition to the photos and videos, the regulator said, Facebook accessed related metadata.
The investigation found Meta asked users to access their camera roll through a single permission that “applies across the entire app covering multiple features with different requirements,” according to a Garante press release .
The permission is preceded by a “non-specific notice” to enable other features, the press release said, failing to make clear to users that they are consenting to suggestions from the camera roll, the regulator said. It also alleged the feature was turned on by default.
“When given in full, such permission allows the app to access the entire photo library on the device, usually on a permanent basis, without the user or [regulators] being able to verify what information is actually being used,” the press release said.
The practice violates Italian data protection regulations safeguarding “the smartphone as part of the individual’s private sphere,” according to a Garate press release.
“Consequently, any access to the information stored on such devices requires free and informed consent, regardless of whether data is transmitted or any harm occurs,” the press release said.
Meta had argued the Garante lacked jurisdiction to issue the fine, but the regulator dismissed that claim.
A Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but told other news outlets in a statement that the company strongly disagrees with the decision and plans to appeal what it called the “disproportionate” fine

As the Defense Department hustles to achieve a clean financial audit opinion by 2028 , officials involved are also transforming the strategy that underpins its complex review process.

During a call with a small group of reporters last week and in subsequent emailed statements to DefenseScoop, senior Pentagon officials discussed how the War Data Platform is informing that work and previewed the DOD’s latest Agency Financial Report ahead of its release on Monday.

“The most significant change for us is our audit strategy. Ultimately, it is what will put us on the path to achieving a clean agency-wide opinion on the [fiscal year] 2028 financial statements,” Jules “Jay” Hurst III, who serves as Pentagon comptroller and DOD’s chief financial officer, said in a statement

Following eight failed attempts to produce an “unmodified” or clean enterprise-wide financial audit opinion, the Pentagon revealed plans this year to overhaul its old methodology, which largely relied on internal IT and accounting controls to verify data from heaps of fragmented systems.

Advertisement

Instead of completing and combining individual audits for the DOD’s many, sprawling components, the department is merging information from 25 different opinions down to eight broader statements, maintaining standalone reviews for major entities, like the military services.

“By consolidating, we reduce the complexity we must manage,” Hurst said in a statement. “We can better share lessons learned and move toward more standardized processes, controls, and systems as we apply those lessons throughout the audit.”

As part of what he referred to as “a fundamental change” in the department’s approach to the audit, Hurst said 2026 marks the last fiscal year that the DOD Office of Inspector General will oversee the effort.

HEADLINE: Base models reproduce HumanEval test cases verbatim; paper reports 96% leakage in one model
PUBLISHED: arXiv v1 stamp "16 Nov 2026"; announced Tue, 17 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500
SOURCES: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21315 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.21315, "Benchleaking Is Accelerating", authors Yiwei Qin, Muhang Xie, Xuefeng Li, Mohan Jiang, Dayuan Fu, Tiantian Mi, Qipeng Guo, Pengfei Liu; affiliations listed in the paper as "Xinxu AI, GAIR" (code: github.com/GAIR-NLP/Benchleaking).
- The paper reports that with few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, "For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base."
- It also cites post-training audits in which "an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none" (attributed in the paper to Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026).
- The authors define an "Anti-Hack score": the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked.
FLAGS: preprint
```

```
SECTION: Research & papers
HEADLINE: Google DeepMind test finds 11 video world models score below random on counterfactual physics flips
PUBLISHED: arXiv v1 stamp 16 Nov 2026; announced Tue, 17 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500 (cross-list)
SOURCES: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19822 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.19822, "The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State". Author affiliations in the paper: Google DeepMind (Lijun Yu, Adams Wei Yu, Ang Cao, Baochen Sun, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Nan Hua, Yuan Hao, Ed H. Chi, Xuezhi Wang, Yinxiao Liu and others), UT Austin (Mi Luo, internship at Google DeepMind), UC Berkeley (Alex Dimakis).
- FlipTest uses 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks, built as visual minimal pairs whose true futures differ.
- The paper reports: "All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing."
- It reports models "flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it", while a vision-language model on the same frames "is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary".
FLAGS: preprint
```

```
SECTION: Research & papers
HEADLINE: Turing Institute replicates MIT claim that a frontier model writes neural-network weights directly
PUBLISHED: arXiv v1 stamp 16 Nov 2026; announced Tue, 17 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500 (cross-list)
SOURCES: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21449 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.21449, "Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers", authors Roksana Goworek, Alexander Hickey, Federico Nanni, Martin O'Reilly, The Alan Turing Institute; the paper describes itself as "a three day sprint" and "a working note".
- The paper reports GPT-6 Astra's directly-written Breakout networks "scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517)", and that "Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens."
- On handwritten digits: "Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%)."
- On reading weights: "Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works."
- The authors report two models "independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states."
FLAGS: preprint, update (follows the MIT weight-space-programming line of work noted on 16 Nov)
```

```

HEADLINE: Agent-to-agent handoff study: chain of eight agents learns as much as one agent in four lives
PUBLISHED: arXiv v1 stamp 16 Nov 2026; announced Tue, 17 Nov 2026 00:00:00 -0500
SOURCES: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18642 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2611.18642, "Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood", sole author Yibo Liu, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications.
- Setup: 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules; one agent playing eight lives with full history vs a chain of eight agents each inheriting a 300-character note.
- The paper reports: "All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives."
- "When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss."
- The paper reports the loss is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, revise the inherited note, or keep a structured ledger.
FLAGS: preprint

Pentagon rebrands principal AI shop as ‘Super Intelligence Office’ - Breaking Defense









Pentagon grapples with growth of artificial intelligence. (Graphic by Breaking Defense, original brain graphic via Getty)

WASHINGTON — The Defense Department announced today that it has redesignated its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO ) as the Super Intelligence Office (SIO).

The DoD said the new name does not reflect a change in mission but rather aligns the office’s designation with the Trump administration’s broader effort to replace references to artificial intelligence with “super intelligence” across the federal government. Cameron Stanley, the department’s top AI official who also helms the SIO, said in a statement that the rebrand also reflects the Pentagon’s priorities moving forward.

“We have moved beyond experimental prototypes. As the Super Intelligence Office, our mission is to harness the full power of sovereign Super Intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain,” Stanley said.

The redesignation follows President Donald Trump’s September announcement that all federal agencies should replace references to AI with the term super intelligence, or SI. At the time, he argued that the word “artificial” made the technology sound fake, despite its growing capabilities.

The terminology shift has raised questions within the tech community, where “superintelligence” has historically referred to a specific , hypothetical form of general artificial intelligence that exceeds overall human intelligence — a capability that does not currently exist.

The Pentagon has been among the federal government’s most aggressive adopters of AI technology, with the CDAO leading efforts to expand its use across military operations and department functions. Those efforts include making artificial intelligence tools more widely available to military personnel through GenAI.mil an enterprise platform providing users access to commercial generative AI models.

The office’s portfolio includes the Maven Smart System , an AI-enabled intelligence and targeting platform, and the War Data Platform, a central data hub formerly known as Advana . The CDAO has also spearheaded numerous exercises and experimentation efforts aimed at integrating artificial intelligence and other advanced capabilities across the department.

The CDAO’s transition to SIO “will roll out across digital systems, enterprise applications and component headquarters over the coming weeks,” the DoD said. “Existing operational programs, industry solicitations and defense partnerships will continue uninterrupted under the new banner.” The department has also launched SI.mil , which will serve as the renamed office’s primary digital domain.

# California sues OpenAI for Hugging Face and other incidents, alleging deception and recklessness
California on Monday sued OpenAI for breaking state law barring companies from engaging in unfair and unlawful business practices due to its alleged failure to stop its AI agents from hacking Hugging Face and deceiving the public about that cyberattack and other similar incidents.
The lawsuit , filed in San Francisco Superior Court, alleges OpenAI officials told state Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office it has lost control over its agents 80-plus times during testing. OpenAI then failed to cooperate with the attorney general’s probe, the office said.
“Rather than take responsibility and be transparent with the public and with regulators
so that these loss-of-control incidents can be analyzed and prevented, OpenAI thwarted the
Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed
information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said.
OpenAI allegedly responded to subpoenas with “just a smattering of publicly available information, self-serving blog posts and redacted copies of a few dozen external communications containing high-level descriptions of select security incidents,” according to the lawsuit.
The artificial intelligence giant is violating California’s Unfair Competition Law, Bonta says, and the company also qualifies as a public nuisance under state law due to its allegedly dangerous practices.
The attorney general is asking a judge to prevent OpenAI from using unfair competition tactics, restore money individuals and organizations lost due to its practices and assess civil penalties of $2,500 per violation against each defendant found at trial to be responsible for breaking the law.
The attack on Hugging Face in July specifically was foreseeable given that OpenAI chose to test models it “knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” according to a Bonta press release .

Abstract: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. # The Permanente Medical Group launches tech incubation company
By
Dave Muoio
Nov 16, 2026 12:08pm
The Permanente Medical Group
Kaiser Permanente
Innovation
startups
The health tech innovation company from Kaiser Permanente's 10,000-strong physician group has "a clear advantage" in validating and scaling new care tools, the organization said. It marked its launch with the unveiling of Wrapt Health, a predictive appointment rescheduling tool, as its first portfolio company. (iStock / Getty Images Plus)
The Permanente Medical Group announced on Monday the launch of a physician-led innovation company it said will strike technology partnerships to co-develop, incubate and launch new enterprise healthcare delivery technologies.
Permanentech—a wholly owned subsidiary of the 10,000-physician medical group, which is itself part of the massive integrated nonprofit Kaiser Permanente—looks to rapidly advance potential new healthcare offerings informed by its frontline physicians and the broader organization’s focus on value-based care.
It marked the launch by announcing its first portfolio company: Wrapt Health, which offers an automated tool that predicts likely missed medical appointments for early outreach and rescheduling. In line with Permanentech’s broader thesis, it was born from a TPMG physician’s experiences, validated within the medical group and so far scaled to 22 sites in Kaiser Permanente’s Northern California region.
“Our clinicians are continuously innovating and refining how we deliver care,” Kenneth Trauner, M.D., CEO of Permanentech and chief innovation officer at TPMG, said in a release. “Permanentech gives them a dedicated resource to rapidly turn their insights and creativity into scalable solutions that benefit both our patients and the wider health care community.”
Permanentech will be focused on technologies and AI-enabled tools addressing patient service, access and quality, TPMG said, with successful products also having the potential to improve “the economics of care delivery.” The business is structured “to move at the pace of the technology industry,” but has “a clear advantage” via its access to TPMG and Kaiser Permanente’s substantial footprint for deployment and validation, it said.
Those efforts will involve both home-grown tools and those developed by established or early-stage partners.
The former will champion physician-developed tools created inside TPMG’s ecosystem as an independent company launches. Starting from the concept phase, that support would include financing as well as clinical and operational validation, as was the case with Wrapt Health.
“Our physicians and care teams see every day where technology can make care better,” Kristine Lee, M.D., an associate executive director and chief transformation officer at TPMG, said. “Permanentech gives them a real hand in building tools that lift administrative burden and give time back to patients. When clinicians help build the tools, those tools fit the way they actually work.”

# Executive Summary

As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks , automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking , the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed.

Key trends over the last quarter include:

-
Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks: Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX , CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

-
Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation: Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.

-
Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse : Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from LLMJacking by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers).

-
LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO): State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution.

-
Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution: Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution.

Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild.

At Google, we are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly. Our multifaceted defense strategy integrates proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, and targeted containment protocols to protect our customers and infrastructure. We continuously harden our models against misuse, mitigate malicious activity through proactive disruption of bad actor projects and accounts, and use our autonomous Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero to operationalize security, continuous monitoring, and responding at machine speed across enterprise environments.

# Multi-Agent Frameworks in Cyber Intrusions

While previous milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, GTIG and Mandiant have now observed multiple threat actors abusing open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions.

Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge.

Figure 1: Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks

In addition to the now highly-publicized pentesting tool ARTEX, threat actors are actively leveraging additional open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. We have also observed evidence of threat actor experimentation with custom-built harnesses. These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics.

GTIG has independently observed open source tools CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.

CAIRN: an open source, multi-agent pentesting framework that implements an OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) loop where specialized agents collaborate via a shared "blackboard" to autonomously navigate from an initial parameter (e.g., a target IP address) toward an operational objective. GTIG observed CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US.

-
CyberStrikeAI : an open source, LLM-native offensive framework which functions as a "single pane of glass" for cyber operations. 91:For instance, in September 2026, GTIG analyzed vulnerability statistics to assess how LLMs are shaping the threat landscape. We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered. Interestingly, while overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, zero-day exploits rose only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August.
97:In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.
99:More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent , that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software. It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention. Along with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, we identified multiple scripts capable of facilitating various post-compromise activities, including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

146:GTIG assesses with high confidence that information operations (IO) threat actors have advanced from initial LLM experimentation to full operational integration. Across all tracked categories—state-sponsored groups, including those attributed to Russia, the PRC, and Iran, commercial "Influence-as-a-Service" (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks—adversaries now routinely embed LLMs into their standard tradecraft to produce synthetic media and automate domain network workflows (e.g., LLM-assisted SEO manipulation, editing and formatting of seeded articles, and automated generation and publishing of influence content). This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is important to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success.
173:GTIG also detected a separate commercial contractor leveraging the Gemini API—as part of a modular, multi-provider AI architecture—during the development of a turnkey IaaS platform engineered to manage over 100,000 accounts across major global platforms. The platform is architected to combine automated agents, anti-detection and device identifier spoofing tools, and cloud phone farms to operate thousands of inauthentic personas across platforms. Observed prompts indicated the actor’s plan to market the tool to both the actor’s domestic government bodies and foreign clients for influence campaign execution.
206:Throughout 2026, Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents where financially motivated actors compromised cloud environments to consume targeted organizations’ cloud compute and/or LLM resource quotas. In the most severe cases, cumulative resource abuse reached $1 million USD before remediation.
226:Threat actors created unauthorized IAM and service accounts or attached administrative policies to service roles. We also observed a threat actor exploit CVE-2026-40217, a sandbox escape in LiteLLM that allows an attacker to elevate limited-access inference keys ("Virtual Keys") into full administrative credentials. Privileged service accounts were sufficient to establish persistence without the use of malware.
244:GTIG analyzed numerous LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces, and found that most services offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken models that advertise support of malicious cyber activity. 29:On October 15, India disclosed its first cyber incident where an AI agent, not a human operator, was responsible. The Government of India issued new guidance on November 4 for auditing AI systems and reporting future incidents. With frontier AI development concentrated in the United States and AI diffusion running through India and the Global South, New Delhi and Washington need to coordinate more in this area. As Prime Minister Modi and President Trump prepare to meet twice before year-end, there is a window for both countries to develop a blueprint for reporting, governing, and containing future incidents.
31:A1: In its October 15 “critical” severity advisory, India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) identified two distinct types of AI agent incidents against Indian technology assets. The first involved AI agents developed by frontier labs that exceeded the scope of their assigned evaluation tasks during model research and development, escaped containment, and accessed live Indian systems, similar to the mid-2026 OpenAI–HuggingFace incident . It is a serious but tractable threat, but is addressable through stronger sandbox design and authorization controls. The second type of attack is more consequential: criminal actors deliberately weaponizing open-source agentic AI tools to conduct “reconnaissance, exploitation, and financially motivated intrusions,” compressing attack timelines from days to hours.
33:A2: In every incident CERT-In documented, the breach came to light either through voluntary disclosures from AI providers or through CERT-In’s own threat hunting. None of the affected organizations detected the intrusions, even as agents accessed and read personal data and confidential business records.

37:A3: The Indian government has been proactively engaged on the threat of AI-enabled cyber. CERT-In’s Comprehensive Cyber Security Audit Policy Guidelines , published in July 2025, established a structured audit framework for critical infrastructure; in April 2026, CERT-In issued a high-severity advisory (CIAD-2026-0020) flagging autonomous reconnaissance and multistage attack orchestration as systemic threats. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman convened the country’s private and public banking executives to level-set on advancing cybersecurity standards after news of the cyber capabilities of Anthropic’s Mythos class of models became public in May 2026. In July 2026, the Reserve Bank of India issued a directive asking banks and nonbanking financial entities to submit a board-approved assessment of their cyber threat landscape. The October 15 CERT-In disclosure has now accelerated these efforts.
38:CERT-In’s November 4 AI Security Auditing Guidelines represent India’s most comprehensive response yet. They call for all AI systems, including those operated by foreign developers, to be classified into four risk tiers: low, moderate, high, and critical. Low-risk systems can self-assess, while moderate- and high-risk systems face annual independent audits. The guidelines also outline requirements for high- and critical-risk systems to face a combination of emergency kill switches, continuous monitoring, and red-team exercises, depending on their tier rankings. For agentic AI systems, they call for all systems to remain within “approved operating parameters” to address sandbox failures. CERT-In also extends its mandate to report all cybersecurity incidents within six hours of any AI-related incidents and demands that enterprises maintain system logs for 180 days.

# Abstract
Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer’s blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.

# Title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
Authors: Yiwei Qin , Muhang Xie , Xuefeng Li , Mohan Jiang , Dayuan Fu , Tiantian Mi , Qipeng Guo , Pengfei Liu
View a PDF of the paper titled Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models, by Yiwei Qin and 7 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

# Title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds
Authors: Yuzhu Ling , Jiale Han , Benyou Wang
View a PDF of the paper titled When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds, by Yuzhu Ling and 2 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.

Abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.

Issues found, most serious first:

1. Intro, host A: "Here's what moved at the frontier of AI since yesterday morning, and **every line traces back to a source we opened**." Directly contradicted by the edition, which repeatedly records sources it could NOT open: "OpenAI's own announcement page could not be opened from this session"; "The BIS document itself could not be opened from this session; bis.gov and commerce.gov press pages returned 403 or 404 and the Federal Register blocked access"; "The CERT-In advisory and the November 4 guidelines could not be opened directly from this session". The script itself contradicts the claim three times later ("We couldn't open OpenAI's own announcement page", "We could not open the rule document itself", "we could not open the underlying advisory"). Not covered by the show-furniture exemption.

2. Benchleaking item, host B: "is about benchmark contamination, and **the authors argue it's got sharply worse**." No support. The edition's closest text is only that the paper "finds some base models write out test examples ... that appear nowhere in their input" and that "The authors call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice." There is no claim anywhere in the edition about contamination worsening over time.

3. Commerce rule item, host A: "It adds licensing for five more countries. Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, which Commerce said present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion." Drops a material qualifier in the same edition sentence: "...and that **for those countries the requirements do not apply to chips destined for companies based in the US**." As delivered, the scope of the new licensing is overstated.

4. Hugging Face / OpenRouter item, host B: "**Price explains a lot of it.**" (followed by host A's "Capability still doesn't."). The edition reports the token-share shift and the price figures as separate facts and never asserts a causal link; this is an explanatory claim the edition does not make.

5. Intro teaser 3, host B: "the Commerce Department issued a rule requiring licences for AI chips that reach data centres serving companies headquartered in China." The summary it must rest on says "...AI chips destined for data centres that **supply more than 12 million total processing performance** to companies headquartered in China **or other D:5 countries**." Dropping the capacity threshold broadens the rule as stated (the threshold is restored later in the body item).

6. CSIS item, host B: "India's emergency response team disclosed its first cyber incident where an AI agent, not a human operator, was responsible. **It was rated critical severity.**" The edition attributes "critical" to the advisory, not to the incident: CERT-In "disclosed, in a 'critical' severity advisory, its first cyber incident in which an AI agent rather than a human operator was responsible."

7. CSIS item, host A: "**And the response was quick.**" A characterisation of CERT-In's pace that the edition does not make; the edition states only the two dates (Oct 15 advisory, Nov 4 guidelines).
